name: Growth, Mastery, and Proficiency
title: Growth, Mastery, and Proficiency
answer: Growth data shows how much students have learned over time, while proficiency data shows where they stand against a standard, and both matter because a school with students starting far behind may show strong growth while proficiency stays low. Reporting both keeps progress visible and keeps gaps from being ignored. Standards mastery dashboards and cohort trend analysis extend this by showing which standards each student has mastered and whether groups of students are doing better over the years.

crumbs.name: Assessment, Data, and the Early Warning System

sections.body: This idea is that a school needs three related views of student learning rather than one. Growth data captures how much a student has learned over time, proficiency data captures where that student stands against a standard, and a school that reports only one of these can mislead itself. A school whose students start far behind may show strong growth even while proficiency remains low, so reporting both keeps progress from being hidden and gaps from being ignored. Standards mastery dashboards add a finer view by showing which standards each student has mastered, which teachers can use to plan small groups and reteaching. Cohort trend analysis adds a longer view by following groups of students over years, so a district can see whether its changes are working.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In day to day teaching, standards mastery dashboards let teachers see which standards each student has mastered and use that to plan small groups and reteaching. The text gives its grade band example in the early years and lower elementary: a district might ask whether students who entered kindergarten in a certain year are doing better in third grade than earlier groups. That kind of cohort trend analysis follows groups of students over years, and AI can help analyze these trends in district data platforms. The results guide long term planning and show whether changes are working. Reporting growth and proficiency side by side is the practice that sits underneath both the dashboards and the trend work.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The supplied text states no evidence label, no study, no figure and no finding for this idea. It describes what growth data, proficiency data, mastery dashboards and cohort trend analysis are for, and how schools and districts use them, but it does not cite research behind them. On the text as given, this idea rests on practice rather than research. The one caution the text does offer is about measurement quality rather than evidence: the dashboards are only as good as the assessments behind them, and a standard measured by a single question gives a weak picture of mastery.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text sets a clear limit on mastery dashboards: they are only as good as the assessments behind them, and a standard measured by a single question gives a weak picture of mastery. That means the quality of the underlying assessment is a decision people have to make, not something the dashboard supplies. The text also keeps the human decisions in human hands, with teachers using the dashboards to plan small groups and reteaching, and with cohort results guiding long term planning rather than replacing it. Reporting both growth and proficiency is itself a guardrail, because it prevents progress from being hidden and prevents gaps from being ignored. Nothing in the text suggests the analysis makes these calls on its own.
